q-343542.worked_solution:
We have the function 

$$
y=({x}^{2}+1)(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{x}.
$$

First, we find the natural logarithm of both sides and use the product rule for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(({x}^{2}+1)(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)+\operatorname{ln}⁡((\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)+x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)+x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\cdot (2x)+(x)^{′}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)+x{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x))}^{′} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+1}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)+x\cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+1}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)+x\operatorname{cot}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+1}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)+x\operatorname{cot}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=({x}^{2}+1)(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =({x}^{2}+1)(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{x}(\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+1}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)+x\operatorname{cot}⁡x) \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{x}(2x+({x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)+x({x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{cot}⁡x) \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{x}(({x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)+2x+x({x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{cot}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =(x)^{′}\operatorname{ln}⁡x+x{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{′}+{[\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)]}^{′} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x+x\cdot \frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}\cdot {sec}^{2}⁡x \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1+\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1+\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

q-138800.problem:
Consider the function $y=({x}^{4}+1){3}^{x+4}.$ The derivative of this function is given by

$$
{y}^{′}={3}^{x+4}\cdot (a{x}^{4}+b{x}^{3}+c).
$$

Find the value of $a+b+c.$
q-138800.worked_solution:
We have the function 

$$
y=({x}^{4}+1){3}^{x+4}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides and use the product rule for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(({x}^{4}+1){3}^{x+4}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4}+1)+\operatorname{ln}⁡({3}^{x+4}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4}+1)+(x+4)\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4}+1)+(x+4)\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =\frac{1}{{x}^{4}+1}\cdot 4{x}^{3}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{4{x}^{3}}{{x}^{4}+1}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\frac{4{x}^{3}}{{x}^{4}+1}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(3))\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=({x}^{4}+1){3}^{x+4}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =({x}^{4}+1){3}^{x+4}(\frac{4{x}^{3}}{{x}^{4}+1}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)) \\  & ={3}^{x+4}(4{x}^{3}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)({x}^{4}+1)) \\  & ={3}^{x+4}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3){x}^{4}+4{x}^{3}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(3))\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
a+b+c=\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+4+\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)=4+2\operatorname{ln}⁡(3).
$$

q-138839.problem:
Consider the function $y=\frac{(x+1)^{{x}^{2}}}{{e}^{2-4x}}.$ The derivative of this function is given by

$$
{y}^{′}=\frac{(x+1)^{{x}^{2}-1}}{{e}^{2-4x}}((x+2)^{2}+g(x)).
$$

Find the function $g(x).$
q-138839.worked_solution:
We have the function 

$$
y=\frac{(x+1)^{{x}^{2}}}{{e}^{2-4x}}.
$$

First, we find the natural logarithm of both sides and use the quotient and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{(x+1)^{{x}^{2}}}{{e}^{2-4x}}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡((x+1)^{{x}^{2}})-\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{2-4x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & ={x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)-(2-4x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)-2+4x) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{x+1}+4 \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+\frac{{x}^{2}}{x+1}+4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+\frac{{x}^{2}}{x+1}+4)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=\frac{(x+1)^{{x}^{2}}}{{e}^{2-4x}}:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{(x+1)^{{x}^{2}}}{{e}^{2-4x}}(2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+\frac{{x}^{2}}{x+1}+4) \\  & =\frac{(x+1)^{{x}^{2}}}{{e}^{2-4x}}(\frac{2x(x+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+{x}^{2}+4(x+1)}{x+1}) \\  & =\frac{(x+1)^{{x}^{2}-1}}{{e}^{2-4x}}(2x(x+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+{x}^{2}+4(x+1)) \\  & =\frac{(x+1)^{{x}^{2}-1}}{{e}^{2-4x}}(2x(x+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+{x}^{2}+4x+4) \\  & =\frac{(x+1)^{{x}^{2}-1}}{{e}^{2-4x}}(2x(x+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+(x+2)^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
g(x)=2x(x+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1).
$$
